title: Visual Data Communication
text:
Overview
A good figure lets someone understand your result in seconds. A poor one hides it, misleads, or simply gets skipped. This course teaches you to design figures with a purpose, and to build them in R (with ggplot2) or Python (with plotnine).
We start from the message and the audience, not the software. You will learn how to choose a chart that fits your question, how to use colour, ordering and labelling to direct attention, and how to produce figures that are honest, accessible and reproducible.






TipLearning objectives




Distinguish between figures for exploring data and figures for explaining it.
Choose a chart type that fits your question and your audience.
Use colour, ordering and labelling to direct attention to your message.
Build, refine and export figures in layers using ggplot2 or plotnine.
Critique any figure using five simple questions.

Both packages implement the same grammar of graphics, so the code looks almost identical in the two languages. The main difference is that Python puts column names in quotes:

RPython

  geom_point()


(ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm"))
 + geom_point())



Learn the ideas once, and you can use them in either language.

title: The design process
text:
Two jobs for a figure
Figures do one of two jobs.
Exploring is for you. You make many quick, rough plots to find out what is in your data. Default settings are fine, and speed matters more than beauty.
Explaining is for someone else. You have found something, and you design one figure to show it clearly, without you there to talk it through.
The most common problem in papers and talks is an exploratory plot shown to an audience as if it were an explanatory figure: default settings, no clear message, and the reader left to work it out.

title: The design process
text:
Why we always explore first
The four small datasets below have the same means, variances, correlation and fitted regression line, to two decimal places (Anscombe 1973). Summarised as numbers they look identical. Plotted, they tell four completely different stories.




Anscombe’s quartet. Each grey line is the same fitted regression: y = 3.0 + 0.5x.



Summary statistics compress your data, and the compression can hide exactly what matters: curves, outliers and clusters. Plot first, then summarise, model or test.

title: The design process
text:
A process for explanatory figures
Most of the work of a good figure happens before any code is written.

Question→ Explore→ Message→ Audience→ Sketch→ Build→ Critique↻


Question and explore. What are you asking, and what does the data actually look like? Chapters 2 to 4 cover this.
Message. Write the message as one sentence: a headline, not a label. “Life expectancy by region” is a label. “Sub-Saharan Africa trails every other region by over 10 years” is a headline. If you cannot write the sentence, the figure cannot show it.
Audience. A reader of your paper can study a figure for minutes. A conference audience sees your slide for thirty seconds while listening to you. A public audience may not know your field’s conventions. The audience decides how much detail, how much text and how big.
Sketch. Draw two or three versions on paper before opening any software. It takes five minutes and stops you spending an hour perfecting the wrong chart.
Build. Only now do you write code. Chapters 5 to 9 cover the techniques.
Critique. Show it to someone, ask what they take away, and go round again.




Three quick sketches for the same data, each with its own headline idea.

title: The design process
text:
How we read figures
We read some visual properties more accurately than others. In classic experiments, people judged values most accurately from position along a common scale, then length, then angle and area, with colour intensity least accurate (Cleveland and McGill 1984). That is why a sorted bar chart beats a pie chart for comparing similar values.
Colour, on the other hand, is seen before we consciously look. A single strong colour among grey draws the eye instantly. That makes colour the best tool for directing attention, and the worst for reading exact values. A recent review of the evidence is given by Franconeri et al. (2021).

title: The design process
text:
Five questions for any figure
Use these to check your own figures and to give feedback to others. Work through them in order: there is no point discussing colours if the message is unclear.


Message. What should someone take away in five seconds?
Audience. Who is it for, and what do they already know?
Chart. Does the chart type fit the question?
Attention. Where does the eye go first? Is that where the message is?
Integrity. Is it honest, readable at its final size, and accessible?








ImportantThe five-second test



Show your figure to someone for five seconds, then hide it. Ask what they remember. If it is not your headline, the figure needs work.

title: The design process
text:
Summary






TipKey points




Exploratory figures are for you; explanatory figures are for your reader. Different rules apply.
Always plot the data before summarising it.
Write the headline first, then design the figure to show it.
Choose the chart by the question: distribution, comparison, relationship, change or part to whole.
Test figures with the five questions and a fresh pair of eyes.







Anscombe, F. J. 1973. “Graphs in Statistical Analysis.” The American Statistician 27 (1): 17–21. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1973.10478966.


Cleveland, William S., and Robert McGill. 1984. “Graphical Perception: Theory, Experimentation, and Application to the Development of Graphical Methods.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 79 (387): 531–54. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478080.


Franconeri, Steven L., Lace M. Padilla, Priti Shah, Jeffrey M. Zacks, and Jessica Hullman. 2021. “The Science of Visual Data Communication: What Works.” Psychological Science in the Public Interest 22 (3): 110–61. https://doi.org/10.1177/15291006211051956.

1.1 The grammar of graphics Core
Both ggplot2 (R) and plotnine (Python) are based on the grammar of graphics (Wickham 2010). Instead of choosing from a menu of chart types, you describe a plot in parts:
You add these parts together with +. Change one part, and only that part of the plot changes. This makes it easy to try ideas quickly.

title: 1  Building a plot in layers
text:
1.3 Layer 1: data and aesthetics Core
Start by saying which data to use, and which variables map to x and y.

RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm))











p = ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm"))
p.show()











We have axes, but no data is drawn. That is because we have not yet said how to draw it.
crumbs: 1  Building a plot in layers

title: 1  Building a plot in layers
text:
1.4 Layer 2: a geometry Core
Add points with geom_point().

RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point()











p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm"))
     + geom_point())
p.show()











We can add more than one geometry. Here is a straight-line trend on top of the points:

RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)











p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm"))
     + geom_point()
     + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False))
p.show()











At first sight, longer bills seem to be shallower. Keep that in mind.
crumbs: 1  Building a plot in layers

title: 1  Building a plot in layers
text:
1.5 Layer 3: mapping colour Core
Now map species to colour, inside aes().

RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)











p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", color="species"))
     + geom_point()
     + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False))
p.show()











Within every species, longer bills are deeper. The overall negative trend was created by mixing three groups with different averages. This is known as Simpson’s paradox, and we found it simply by adding one aesthetic. It is a good example of why exploring your data matters: it can change your conclusion, not just your figure.






ImportantDesign principle: aesthetics are inherited



Anything inside ggplot(aes(...)) applies to every layer. That is why both the points and the trend lines were coloured by species, and why we got one trend line per species.

title: 1  Building a plot in layers
text:
1.6 Mapping versus setting Core
This is the most common source of confusion for beginners.

Mapping links a visual property to a variable. It goes inside aes().
Setting gives a visual property one fixed value. It goes outside aes().


RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 2, alpha = 0.6)











p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm"))
     + geom_point(color="steelblue", size=2, alpha=0.6))
p.show()











Here every point is the same blue, at the same size, partly transparent. If you accidentally write aes(colour = "steelblue"), the software treats "steelblue" as a tiny dataset with one category, and you get a legend with a single entry and a default colour. Try it to see.

title: 1  Building a plot in layers
text:
1.7 Layer 4: labels and theme Core
Readable labels and a cleaner theme make a big difference. Notice the title is a headline: it says what to notice.

RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Within each species, longer bills are deeper",
       x = "Bill length (mm)",
       y = "Bill depth (mm)",
       colour = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", color="species"))
     + geom_point(alpha=0.8)
     + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=False)
     + labs(title="Within each species, longer bills are deeper",
            x="Bill length (mm)",
            y="Bill depth (mm)",
            color="Species")
     + theme_minimal(base_size=13))
p.show()

1.10 Summary






TipKey points




A plot is built from data, aesthetics, geometries, scales and a theme, added together with +.
Variables are mapped inside aes(); fixed values are set outside it.
Aesthetics in the main ggplot() call are inherited by every layer.
Adding one aesthetic can change what you conclude, so explore before you explain.
Save plots with an explicit width, height and resolution.

title: 2  Distributions
text:
2.1 Why distributions matter
A mean is one number. It cannot tell you whether values are symmetric or skewed, whether there are clusters, or whether one extreme value is pulling everything along. The two figures above show four groups with the same mean and standard error. As bars they look identical. As dots, they are completely different.
Bar charts of means with error bars are still common for continuous data, despite hiding exactly these patterns (Weissgerber et al. 2015). This chapter shows better options.

title: 2  Distributions
text:
2.2 Load packages and data
We use the finches data: beak and body measurements of Darwin’s finches, in four groups defined by when they were sampled (early or late) and beak shape (blunt or pointed).

RPython



library(tidyverse)

finches <- read_csv("data/finches.csv")
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")




import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

finches = pd.read_csv("data/finches.csv")
penguins = pd.read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

title: 2  Distributions
text:
2.3 One variable: histograms Core
A histogram splits the values into bins and counts how many fall in each.

RPython



ggplot(finches, aes(x = bdepth)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Beak depth (mm)", y = "Number of finches")











p = (ggplot(finches, aes(x="bdepth"))
     + geom_histogram(binwidth=0.25, fill="grey", color="white")
     + labs(x="Beak depth (mm)", y="Number of finches"))
p.show()

















ImportantDesign principle: always choose the bin width



The default number of bins is rarely right. Too few bins hide structure; too many turn the histogram into noise. Try a few values and choose one that matches the precision of your measurements. Here, beak depth is measured to about 0.1 mm, so bins of 0.25 mm are reasonable.

title: 2  Distributions
text:
2.4 Comparing groups Core
To compare the four groups, we can split the histogram into panels with facet_wrap(). Putting the panels in one column lines up the x axes, so the shifts between groups are easy to see.

RPython



ggplot(finches, aes(x = bdepth)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Beak depth (mm)", y = "Number of finches")











p = (ggplot(finches, aes(x="bdepth"))
     + geom_histogram(binwidth=0.25, fill="grey", color="white")
     + facet_wrap("group", ncol=1)
     + labs(x="Beak depth (mm)", y="Number of finches")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 5)))
p.show()











Histograms work well for one to four groups. With more groups, the options below are easier to compare.

title: 2  Distributions
section: 2.5 Box plots, violins and points Core
text:
2.5 Box plots, violins and points Core
A box plot summarises each group with five numbers: the median (thick line), the middle 50% of values (the box) and the range of typical values (the whiskers), with unusual values drawn as points.

RPython



ggplot(finches, aes(x = group, y = bdepth)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Beak depth (mm)")











p = (ggplot(finches, aes(x="group", y="bdepth"))
     + geom_boxplot()
     + labs(x="", y="Beak depth (mm)"))
p.show()











A box plot still hides how many observations there are and how they are spread inside the box. Adding the raw points fixes that. geom_jitter() spreads the points sideways slightly so they do not sit on top of each other.

RPython



ggplot(finches, aes(x = group, y = bdepth)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0072CF") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Beak depth (mm)")











p = (ggplot(finches, aes(x="group", y="bdepth"))
     + geom_boxplot(outlier_shape="", width=0.5)
     + geom_jitter(width=0.15, alpha=0.5, color="#0072CF")
     + labs(x="", y="Beak depth (mm)"))
p.show()











We turned off the box plot’s own outlier points, because the jittered points already show every observation.
A violin plot shows the full shape of each distribution, like a smoothed histogram mirrored on both sides. It is useful for larger samples, where individual points become crowded.

RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "grey90") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Flipper length (mm)")











p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="species", y="flipper_length_mm"))
     + geom_violin(fill="#E5E5E5")
     + geom_boxplot(width=0.1, outlier_shape="")
     + labs(x="", y="Flipper length (mm)"))
p.show()

section: 2.7 Show the data, not just the mean Extension
text:
2.7 Show the data, not just the mean Extension
If you need to show a mean and an uncertainty interval, show it on top of the data rather than instead of it. stat_summary() calculates the summary for you.

RPython



ggplot(finches, aes(x = group, y = bdepth)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4, colour = "grey50") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, colour = "#D6083B", size = 0.8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Beak depth (mm)",
       caption = "Red points: mean with 95% confidence interval")











p = (ggplot(finches, aes(x="group", y="bdepth"))
     + geom_jitter(width=0.15, alpha=0.4, color="grey")
     + stat_summary(fun_data="mean_cl_normal", color="#D6083B", size=0.8)
     + labs(x="", y="Beak depth (mm)",
            caption="Red points: mean with 95% confidence interval"))
p.show()

title: 2  Distributions
text:
2.8 Exercises






ExerciseBin widths







Level: 
Make a histogram of penguin body mass (body_mass_g). Try bin widths of 50, 200 and 1000 grams. Which shows the shape best, and why?






AnswerAnswer








RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 200, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Number of penguins")











p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="body_mass_g"))
     + geom_histogram(binwidth=200, fill="grey", color="white")
     + labs(x="Body mass (g)", y="Number of penguins"))
p.show()











At 50 g the histogram is noisy, and at 1000 g almost everything is in three bars. Around 200 g shows a clear shape, with a hint of two peaks: a clue that there are groups in the data (the species).
















ExerciseCompare species







Level: 
Compare body mass between the three penguin species using a box plot with jittered points. Colour the points by sex. What do you notice?






AnswerAnswer








RPython



penguins |>
  drop_na(sex) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = sex), width = 0.15, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Sex")











p = (ggplot(penguins.dropna(subset=["sex"]), aes(x="species", y="body_mass_g"))
     + geom_boxplot(outlier_shape="", width=0.5)
     + geom_jitter(aes(color="sex"), width=0.15, alpha=0.7)
     + labs(x="", y="Body mass (g)", color="Sex"))
p.show()











Gentoo penguins are much heavier than the other two species. Within each species, males tend to be heavier than females, which is why some boxes look wide.
















ExerciseRemake a dynamite plot Extension







Level: 
The code below makes a bar chart of mean flipper length with standard error bars. Remake it so that it shows every observation as well as the mean.
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            se = sd(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n())) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = mean)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.2)






AnswerAnswer








RPython



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, colour = "#D6083B", size = 0.6) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Flipper length (mm)")











p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="species", y="flipper_length_mm"))
     + geom_jitter(width=0.15, alpha=0.3)
     + stat_summary(fun_data="mean_se", color="#D6083B", size=0.6)
     + labs(x="", y="Flipper length (mm)"))
p.show()











The new version shows the same means, plus the spread, the sample size and any unusual values. Notice that the y axis no longer needs to start at zero, because we are reading positions, not bar lengths.

title: 2  Distributions
text:
2.9 Summary






TipKey points




Means and error bars can hide skew, clusters and outliers. Show the data where you can.
Histograms need a deliberate bin width.
Box plots summarise; adding points shows what is underneath.
Choose the plot by sample size and number of groups.







Weissgerber, Tracey L., Natasa M. Milic, Stacey J. Winham, and Vesna D. Garovic. 2015. “Beyond Bar and Line Graphs: Time for a New Data Presentation Paradigm.” PLOS Biology 13 (4): e1002128. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002128.

title: 3  Relationships
text:
3.1 Load packages and data
We use the Gapminder data for 2010: one row per country.

title: 3  Relationships
text:
RPython



library(tidyverse)

gapminder <- read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv")




import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

gapminder = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv")

title: 3  Relationships
text:
3.2 The scatter plot Core
A scatter plot puts one variable on each axis and draws one point per observation. It is the default choice when you ask “does one thing go with another?”

RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point()











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_point())
p.show()











Most countries are squashed into the left of the plot, because a few very rich countries stretch the x axis. Income is a classic skewed variable.

title: 3  Relationships
section: 3.3 Log scales for skewed data Core
text:
3.3 Log scales for skewed data Core
On a log scale, each step along the axis is a multiplication rather than an addition: 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000. This spreads out the crowded low values.

RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_point()
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)"))
p.show()











The relationship now looks close to a straight line: each doubling of income is associated with a similar gain in life expectancy.






ImportantDesign principle: say when an axis is on a log scale



Many readers assume a linear axis. Write “log scale” in the axis label, and use readable tick labels such as $1,000 rather than 3.

title: 3  Relationships
text:
3.4 Overplotting Core
When points overlap, dense areas look the same as sparse ones. Transparency (alpha) helps: overlapping points build up darker areas.

RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.4, colour = "#003E72") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_point(size=2.5, alpha=0.4, color="#003E72")
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)"))
p.show()











With thousands of points, consider geom_bin_2d() or geom_hex(), which count points in small tiles, or a density contour.

title: 3  Relationships
text:
3.5 Trend lines Core
geom_smooth() adds a fitted line. method = "lm" fits a straight line; the default in R is a flexible curve (loess), which is useful for spotting non-linear patterns. The grey band is a confidence interval for the fitted line.

RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#D6083B") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_point(alpha=0.4)
     + geom_smooth(method="lm", color="#D6083B")
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)"))
p.show()











A trend line is a model. Only add one if it helps the message, and say what kind of line it is in the legend or caption. This course is about showing relationships; to calculate and test them, see Core statistics 3: correlations.

title: 3  Relationships
text:
3.6 Adding a third variable Core
Colour is the most common way to add a grouping variable. With six regions, though, the plot quickly becomes hard to read: six colours to tell apart and a legend to decode.

RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)", colour = NULL)











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy", color="region"))
     + geom_point(size=2)
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)", color=""))
p.show()











Two better options, depending on the message:

Highlight one group and make the rest grey. This is covered in Colour with purpose.
Split into small multiples, one panel per group, using facet_wrap().


RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(data = select(gapminder, -region), colour = "grey85", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072CF", size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")











background = gapminder.drop(columns="region")

p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_point(data=background, color="#D9D9D9", size=1.2)
     + geom_point(color="#0072CF", size=1.5)
     + facet_wrap("region")
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 5)))
p.show()











The trick here is the first layer. It uses a copy of the data with the region column removed, so facet_wrap() cannot split it, and every panel shows all the countries in light grey. Each region is then drawn on top in blue, compared against the whole world.

title: 3  Relationships
text:
3.7 Exercises






ExerciseChildren and child mortality







Level: 
Plot the number of children per woman (x) against child mortality (y). Is a log scale useful for either axis? Add a sensible title.






AnswerAnswer








RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = children_per_woman, y = child_mortality)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Where women have more children, more children die young",
       x = "Children per woman", y = "Child deaths per 1,000 births (log scale)")











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="children_per_woman", y="child_mortality"))
     + geom_point(alpha=0.6)
     + scale_y_log10()
     + labs(title="Where women have more children, more children die young",
            x="Children per woman", y="Child deaths per 1,000 births (log scale)"))
p.show()











Child mortality is skewed, so a log scale on y spreads out the low values. Children per woman is not strongly skewed, so a linear axis is fine. Be careful with the headline: this is a correlation across countries, not evidence that one causes the other.
















ExerciseSize as a channel







Level: 
Map population to point size in the income and life expectancy plot. What does it add? What problems does it introduce?






AnswerAnswer








RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy, size = population)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#003E72") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy", size="population"))
     + geom_point(alpha=0.5, color="#003E72")
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + scale_size_area(max_size=15)
     + guides(size=None)
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)"))
p.show()











Size shows which countries affect the most people. But area is a channel we read inaccurately, large bubbles hide small ones, and you need a legend to decode it. Use it for a rough impression, not for precise comparisons. scale_size_area() makes the bubble area, rather than its radius, proportional to the value, which is the honest choice.

title: 3  Relationships
text:
3.8 Summary






TipKey points




Scatter plots are the default for relationships between two numeric variables.
Use a log scale for skewed variables, and label it clearly.
Transparency reduces overplotting.
A trend line is a model: add it only when it supports the message.
With many groups, highlight one or use small multiples instead of many colours.

title: 4  Change over time
text:
4.1 Load packages and data
We now use Gapminder data for every year from 1960 to 2010.

title: 4  Change over time
text:
RPython



library(tidyverse)

gap_years <- read_csv("data/gapminder_1960_2010.csv")




import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

gap_years = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_1960_2010.csv")

title: 4  Change over time
text:
4.2 One line Core
Lines connect observations in order, which suits anything measured along an ordered scale such as time. Let’s look at a single country.

RPython



gap_years |>
  filter(country == "Rwanda") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#003E72") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)")











rwanda = gap_years[gap_years["country"] == "Rwanda"]

p = (ggplot(rwanda, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_line(size=1, color="#003E72")
     + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.5)))
p.show()











The sharp fall in the early 1990s is the 1994 genocide. A line chart makes events like this obvious in a way a table never could.






NoteDo I need an x axis label?



When the axis shows years, the label “year” adds nothing, so we removed it with x = NULL (R) or x="" (Python). Remove labels that only repeat what the tick marks already say.

title: 4  Change over time
text:
4.3 Several lines Core
To draw one line per country, map country to group. Without it, the software would join all the points into one zigzag.

RPython



countries <- c("Rwanda", "Brazil", "India", "United Kingdom")

gap_years |>
  filter(country %in% countries) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)", colour = NULL)











countries = ["Rwanda", "Brazil", "India", "United Kingdom"]
four = gap_years[gap_years["country"].isin(countries)]

p = (ggplot(four, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy", color="country"))
     + geom_line(size=1)
     + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()











Mapping colour also sets the groups, so here we did not need group separately.

title: 4  Change over time
text:
4.4 Too many lines Core
With every country, the plot turns into spaghetti.

RPython



ggplot(gap_years, aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy, group = country)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)")











p = (ggplot(gap_years, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy", group="country"))
     + geom_line(alpha=0.3)
     + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()











We can see the overall trend upwards and a few dramatic dips, but we cannot follow any single country. There are three good ways out.

4.4.1 Option 1: highlight a few
Draw everything in light grey for context, then draw the lines you care about on top.

RPython



focus <- gap_years |> filter(country %in% c("Rwanda", "Cambodia"))

ggplot(gap_years, aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy, group = country)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey85") +
  geom_line(data = focus, aes(colour = country), linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Cambodia = "#EA7125", Rwanda = "#D6083B")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)", colour = NULL)











focus = gap_years[gap_years["country"].isin(["Rwanda", "Cambodia"])]

p = (ggplot(gap_years, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy", group="country"))
     + geom_line(color="#D9D9D9")
     + geom_line(data=focus, mapping=aes(color="country"), size=1.2)
     + scale_color_manual(values={"Cambodia": "#EA7125", "Rwanda": "#D6083B"})
     + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)", color="")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()













4.4.2 Option 2: small multiples
Split the data into one panel per region with facet_wrap(). All panels share the same axes, so they can be compared at a glance.

RPython



ggplot(gap_years, aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy, group = country)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#0072CF") +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1960, 1985, 2010)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)")











p = (ggplot(gap_years, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy", group="country"))
     + geom_line(alpha=0.4, color="#0072CF")
     + facet_wrap("region")
     + scale_x_continuous(breaks=[1960, 1985, 2010])
     + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 5)))
p.show()













4.4.3 Option 3: summarise
Sometimes the message is about groups, not individual countries. Calculate a summary per group and year, then plot a few lines.

RPython



region_means <- gap_years |>
  group_by(region, year) |>
  summarise(life_expectancy = mean(life_expectancy, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(region_means, aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy, colour = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean life expectancy (years)", colour = NULL)











region_means = (gap_years
                .groupby(["region", "year"], as_index=False)["life_expectancy"]
                .mean())

p = (ggplot(region_means, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy", color="region"))
     + geom_line(size=1.1)
     + labs(x="", y="Mean life expectancy (years)", color="")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()











This is far easier to read, but remember what the summary hides: the spread between countries and events like the ones in Rwanda and Cambodia. Six lines with a legend is still hard work. In Labels, titles and annotation we replace the legend with labels at the end of each line.

title: 4  Change over time
text:
4.5 Exercises






ExerciseIncome over time







Level: 
Plot income per person over time for China, India and the United States. Use a log scale on the y axis. Why does a log scale make sense for growth?






AnswerAnswer








RPython



gap_years |>
  filter(country %in% c("China", "India", "United States")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = income_per_person, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Income per person (log scale)", colour = NULL)

p = (ggplot(three, aes(x="year", y="income_per_person", color="country"))

p.show()











On a log scale, a constant growth rate appears as a straight line, and the slope shows how fast an economy grows, whatever its starting size. China’s steep slope after 1980 stands out, even though the United States is far richer throughout.
















ExerciseHighlight in context







Level: 
Pick one region. Draw every country in the world in light grey, and the countries in your chosen region in a strong colour on top. Write a headline title.

title: 5  Ranking and ordering
text:
5.3 Sort by value Core
By default, categories appear in alphabetical order, which is almost never what the reader needs. Sorting by value turns a lookup table into a ranking.

RPython


In R, fct_reorder() reorders a categorical variable by another variable.

ggplot(region_le, aes(x = life_expectancy, y = fct_reorder(region, life_expectancy))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Mean life expectancy (years)", y = NULL)








Putting the categories on the y axis gives horizontal bars, so long names have room.


In Python, set the order by turning the column into an ordered category. plotnine draws horizontal bars with coord_flip().

order = region_le.sort_values("life_expectancy")["region"]
region_le["region"] = pd.Categorical(region_le["region"], categories=order)

p = (ggplot(region_le, aes(x="region", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_col()
     + coord_flip()
     + labs(x="", y="Mean life expectancy (years)")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.5)))
p.show()








Note that with coord_flip() the x and y labels refer to the original axes, before flipping.









ImportantDesign principle: order is information



Sort by the value unless the categories have a natural order of their own, such as age groups, months, or dose levels. Then keep the natural order.

title: 5  Ranking and ordering
text:
5.4 Dot plots and lollipops Core
Bars must start at zero, because we read their length. When all values are far from zero, or there are many categories, a dot plot uses less ink and lets the axis focus on the range that matters.

RPython



ggplot(region_le, aes(x = life_expectancy, y = fct_reorder(region, life_expectancy))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 55, xend = life_expectancy, yend = region), colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 4, colour = "#003E72") +
  labs(x = "Mean life expectancy (years)", y = NULL)











p = (ggplot(region_le, aes(x="region", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_segment(aes(xend="region", y=55, yend="life_expectancy"), color="#B3B3B3")
     + geom_point(size=4, color="#003E72")
     + coord_flip()
     + labs(x="", y="Mean life expectancy (years)")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.5)))
p.show()











This is a lollipop chart: a dot plot with a thin line to guide the eye. Because the stick starts at 55 rather than 0, the length of the stick means nothing on its own. That is fine for dots and lollipops, but not for bars.

title: 5  Ranking and ordering
text:
5.5 Top and bottom Extension
With many categories, show only the ones that matter for the message, and say so in the title.

RPython



gapminder |>
  slice_max(child_mortality, n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = child_mortality, y = fct_reorder(country, child_mortality))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#D6083B") +
  labs(title = "The ten countries with the highest child mortality in 2010",
       x = "Deaths before age 5 per 1,000 births", y = NULL)











top10 = gapminder.nlargest(10, "child_mortality").copy()
order = top10.sort_values("child_mortality")["country"]
top10["country"] = pd.Categorical(top10["country"], categories=order)

p = (ggplot(top10, aes(x="country", y="child_mortality"))
     + geom_col(fill="#D6083B")
     + coord_flip()
     + labs(title="The ten countries with the highest child mortality in 2010",
            x="", y="Deaths before age 5 per 1,000 births")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()

title: 5  Ranking and ordering
text:
5.6 Parts of a whole Extension
Pie charts encode values as angles and areas, which we compare poorly. For shares, a single stacked bar or a set of sorted bars is usually clearer. Here is the share of countries in each income group, by region.

RPython



gapminder |>
  mutate(income_groups = fct_relevel(income_groups, "low_income", "lower_middle_income",
                                     "upper_middle_income", "high_income")) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = region, fill = income_groups)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues",
                    labels = c("Low", "Lower middle", "Upper middle", "High")) +
  labs(x = "Share of countries", y = NULL, fill = "Income group")











levels = ["low_income", "lower_middle_income", "upper_middle_income", "high_income"]
gapminder["income_groups"] = pd.Categorical(gapminder["income_groups"], categories=levels)

p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="region", fill="income_groups"))
     + geom_bar(position="fill")
     + coord_flip()
     + scale_y_continuous(labels=lambda breaks: [f"{b:.0%}" for b in breaks])
     + scale_fill_brewer(palette="Blues",
                         labels=["Low", "Lower middle", "Upper middle", "High"])
     + labs(x="", y="Share of countries", fill="Income group")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()











Income groups have a natural order, so we set it explicitly and used a sequential palette (light to dark) to match. See Colour with purpose.

Level: 
Make a horizontal bar chart of median income per person by region, sorted from highest to lowest.






AnswerAnswer

  group_by(region) |>

income = gapminder.groupby("region", as_index=False)["income_per_person"].median()
order = income.sort_values("income_per_person")["region"]
income["region"] = pd.Categorical(income["region"], categories=order)

p.show()











In R, sorting with fct_reorder() puts the largest value at the top of a horizontal bar chart, because the y axis counts upwards from the bottom.
















ExerciseBars or dots?







Level: 
Make a dot plot of mean bill length per penguin species. Then make it as a bar chart. Which works better, and why?






AnswerAnswer








RPython



penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(bill = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill, y = fct_reorder(species, bill))) +

order = bill.sort_values("bill_length_mm")["species"]

title: 5  Ranking and ordering
text:
5.8 Summary






TipKey points




geom_bar() counts rows; geom_col() draws values you have calculated.
Sort categories by value unless they have a natural order.
Horizontal bars give long labels room.
Bars start at zero; dot plots and lollipops do not need to.
Prefer sorted or stacked bars to pie charts for comparing shares.

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
6.1 Three kinds of palette Core
Using the wrong kind misleads the reader. A qualitative palette on a numeric variable suggests categories that do not exist; a sequential palette on categories suggests an order that does not exist.

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
Palette
Data
Examples




Sequential
A quantity from low to high
Concentration, count, income


Diverging
Values either side of a meaningful midpoint
Change from baseline, correlation, temperature anomaly


Qualitative
Unordered categories
Species, treatment, region

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
6.2 Load packages and data

RPython



library(tidyverse)

gapminder <- read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv")
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")




import pandas as pd
from plotnine import *

gapminder = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv")
penguins = pd.read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
6.3 Qualitative colours you choose Core
The default colours are designed to be evenly spaced in hue, not to be easy to tell apart for everyone. The Okabe and Ito palette was designed to remain distinguishable for people with the common forms of colour vision deficiency (Okabe and Ito 2008). Set your own colours with scale_colour_manual().

RPython



okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
               "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000")

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = okabe_ito) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Flipper length (mm)", colour = "Species")











okabe_ito = ["#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
             "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000"]

p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="flipper_length_mm", color="species"))
     + geom_point(size=2, alpha=0.8)
     + scale_color_manual(values=okabe_ito)
     + labs(x="Bill length (mm)", y="Flipper length (mm)", color="Species"))
p.show()











To give specific colours to specific groups, use a named vector (R) or dictionary (Python), for example c(Adelie = "#E69F00", ...). Then the colours stay the same in every figure, even if a group is missing from one of them.

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
6.4 Sequential colours and viridis Core
For a continuous variable, use a palette that changes evenly in lightness. The viridis family was designed for this: it is perceptually even, works in greyscale, and is readable with colour vision deficiency.

RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy, colour = child_mortality)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       colour = "Child deaths\nper 1,000")











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy", color="child_mortality"))
     + geom_point(size=2.5)
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + scale_color_cmap("viridis_r")
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)",
            color="Child deaths\nper 1,000"))
p.show()











We reversed the palette so that darker means more child deaths, which matches how most people read darkness.

6.4.1 Why not a rainbow?
Rainbow colour maps change lightness unevenly, so we see sharp boundaries where the data changes smoothly, and they fail for colour vision deficiency (Crameri et al. 2020). The two maps below show the same smooth surface.



The same volcano surface with a rainbow palette (left) and viridis (right).

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
6.5 Diverging colours Core
A diverging palette uses two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint. It is right when the midpoint means something, such as zero change or zero correlation. Here is a correlation matrix of the Gapminder variables.

RPython



vars <- c("children_per_woman", "child_mortality", "life_expectancy",
          "income_per_person", "population")

cor_long <- cor(gapminder[vars]) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r")

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#0072B2", mid = "white", high = "#D55E00",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))











vars_ = ["children_per_woman", "child_mortality", "life_expectancy",
         "income_per_person", "population"]

cor_long = (gapminder[vars_].corr()
            .reset_index(names="var1")
            .melt(id_vars="var1", var_name="var2", value_name="r"))
cor_long["label"] = cor_long["r"].round(2)

p = (ggplot(cor_long, aes(x="var1", y="var2", fill="r"))
     + geom_tile(color="white")
     + geom_text(aes(label="label"), size=9)
     + scale_fill_gradient2(low="#0072B2", mid="white", high="#D55E00",
                            midpoint=0, limits=(-1, 1))
     + labs(x="", y="", fill="Correlation")
     + theme(axis_text_x=element_text(rotation=30, ha="right"),
             figure_size=(7, 4.6)))
p.show()











Setting limits to -1 and 1 keeps white at exactly zero, so the colours are honest even if the strongest correlation is only 0.6.

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
6.6 Grey first, then highlight Core
This is the most useful colour technique for explanatory figures. Make everything grey, then add one strong colour only where you want attention. Create a true or false column for the group of interest, and map colour to it.

RPython



gapminder |>
  mutate(focus = region == "Sub-Saharan Africa") |>
  arrange(focus) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy, colour = focus)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey75", "#D6083B"), guide = "none") +
  annotate("text", x = 1000, y = 77, label = "Sub-Saharan Africa",
           colour = "#D6083B", fontface = "bold", hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_minimal()











gapminder["focus"] = gapminder["region"] == "Sub-Saharan Africa"
ordered = gapminder.sort_values("focus")

p = (ggplot(ordered, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy", color="focus"))
     + geom_point(size=2.5)
     + scale_color_manual(values=["#BFBFBF", "#D6083B"], guide=None)
     + annotate("text", x=1000, y=77, label="Sub-Saharan Africa",
                color="#D6083B", fontweight="bold", ha="left")
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)")
     + theme_minimal())
p.show()











Two details make this work. Sorting by focus draws the highlighted points last, so they sit on top of the grey ones. And the label is written on the plot in the highlight colour, so there is no legend to decode.

title: 6  Colour with purpose
section: 6.7 Check for colour vision deficiency Extension
text:
6.7 Check for colour vision deficiency Extension
About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of colour vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green. Check your figures with a simulator.



Red, green and orange (left pair) become hard to separate with deuteranopia. The Okabe and Ito palette (right pair) stays distinct.



RPython


The colorspace package can simulate how a set of colours looks with each type of colour vision deficiency.

library(colorspace)

my_colours <- c("#D6083B", "#55A51C", "#EA7125")
swatchplot("Original" = my_colours,
           "Deuteranopia" = deutan(my_colours),
           "Protanopia" = protan(my_colours))










There is no simulator built into plotnine. Save your figure and check it with a free online tool such as Coblis, or install the colorspacious package to simulate colours in code.



The simplest protection is not to rely on colour alone: add direct labels, or use shape as a second cue.

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
6.8 Exercises






ExerciseName your colours







Level: 
Plot penguin bill length against bill depth, coloured by species, using a named set of three colours of your choice from the Okabe and Ito palette.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = species_cols) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)", colour = NULL)











species_cols = {"Adelie": "#E69F00", "Chinstrap": "#CC79A7", "Gentoo": "#009E73"}

p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", color="species"))

     + labs(x="Bill length (mm)", y="Bill depth (mm)", color=""))

Level: 
Remake the plot so that only Gentoo penguins are coloured, with the others in light grey. Label the group directly instead of using a legend, and write a headline.






AnswerAnswer








RPython



penguins |>
  mutate(focus = species == "Gentoo") |>

  annotate("text", x = 55, y = 14, label = "Gentoo", colour = "#009E73",
           fontface = "bold", hjust = 1) +
  labs(title = "Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills",
       x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()











penguins["focus"] = penguins["species"] == "Gentoo"

p = (ggplot(penguins.sort_values("focus"),
            aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", color="focus"))
     + geom_point(size=2)
     + scale_color_manual(values=["#CCCCCC", "#009E73"], guide=None)
     + annotate("text", x=55, y=14, label="Gentoo", color="#009E73",
                fontweight="bold", ha="right")
     + labs(title="Gentoo penguins have long but shallow bills",
            x="Bill length (mm)", y="Bill depth (mm)")
     + theme_minimal())
p.show()

title: 6  Colour with purpose
text:
6.9 Summary






TipKey points




Sequential palettes for amounts, diverging palettes around a meaningful midpoint, qualitative palettes for categories.
Avoid rainbow colour maps; use viridis or similar.
Choose colour-blind safe colours, and never rely on colour alone.
Grey everything first, then highlight what matters.







Crameri, Fabio, Grace E. Shephard, and Philip J. Heron. 2020. “The Misuse of Colour in Science Communication.” Nature Communications 11: 5444. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19160-7.


Okabe, Masataka, and Kei Ito. 2008. Color Universal Design (CUD): How to Make Figures and Presentations That Are Friendly to Colorblind People. https://jfly.uni-koeln.de/color/.

RPython

from plotnine import *

gap_years = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_1960_2010.csv")

title: 7  Labels, titles and annotation
text:
7.2 Titles that say something Core
labs() sets the title, subtitle, caption and axis labels in one place.

Title: the headline. What should the reader notice?
Subtitle: what is measured, where and when.
Caption: the source, and any notes on method.
Axis labels: plain words with units, never raw variable names.


RPython



ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = children_per_woman, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Where families are smaller, people live longer",
       subtitle = "167 countries, 2010",
       caption = "Source: Gapminder",
       x = "Children per woman",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)")











p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="children_per_woman", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_point(alpha=0.6)
     + labs(title="Where families are smaller, people live longer",
            subtitle="167 countries, 2010",
            caption="Source: Gapminder",
            x="Children per woman",
            y="Life expectancy (years)")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 4.4)))
p.show()

















NoteTitles in papers



Journals usually want the headline in the figure legend rather than on the figure. The principle is the same: the first sentence of the legend should state the message. For talks and posters, put the headline on the figure itself.

title: 7  Labels, titles and annotation
section: 7.3 Direct labels instead of legends Core
text:
7.3 Direct labels instead of legends Core
For line charts, labelling each line where it ends removes the need for a legend. The approach is the same in both languages: make a small table of the last point of each line, then draw text there.

RPython



region_years <- gap_years |>
  group_by(region, year) |>
  summarise(life_expectancy = mean(life_expectancy, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

line_ends <- region_years |> filter(year == max(year))

ggplot(region_years, aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy, colour = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = line_ends, aes(label = region),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1.5, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1960, 2010, 10),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.45))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











region_years = (gap_years
                .groupby(["region", "year"], as_index=False)["life_expectancy"]
                .mean())
line_ends = region_years[region_years["year"] == region_years["year"].max()]

p = (ggplot(region_years, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy", color="region"))
     + geom_line(size=1.1)
     + geom_text(line_ends, aes(label="region"),
                 ha="left", nudge_x=1.5, size=10, fontweight="bold")
     + scale_x_continuous(breaks=range(1960, 2011, 10), limits=(1960, 2035))
     + labs(x="", y="Mean life expectancy (years)")
     + theme_minimal()
     + theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(7, 4.4)))
p.show()











We extended the x axis to make room for the labels. Some labels may overlap where lines end close together. You can nudge individual labels by hand, or in R use the ggrepel package (geom_text_repel()), which moves labels apart automatically.

title: 7  Labels, titles and annotation
text:
7.4 Annotation Core
Annotations explain why the data looks the way it does. annotate() adds a single piece of text, a line or a shape at a position you choose.

RPython



rwanda <- gap_years |> filter(country == "Rwanda")

ggplot(rwanda, aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#003E72") +
  annotate("segment", x = 1985, xend = 1993.5, y = 25, yend = 15,
           colour = "grey40", arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = 1984, y = 26, label = "1994 genocide", hjust = 1, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "Rwanda: life expectancy collapsed in 1994 and then recovered",
       x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_minimal()











rwanda = gap_years[gap_years["country"] == "Rwanda"]

p = (ggplot(rwanda, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_line(size=1.1, color="#003E72")
     + annotate("segment", x=1985, xend=1993.5, y=25, yend=15,
                color="#666666", arrow=arrow(length=0.08))
     + annotate("text", x=1984, y=26, label="1994 genocide", ha="right", color="#4D4D4D")
     + labs(title="Rwanda: life expectancy collapsed in 1994 and then recovered",
            x="", y="Life expectancy (years)")
     + theme_minimal()
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()

title: 7  Labels, titles and annotation
text:
7.5 Themes and clutter Core
Everything that is not data (grid lines, borders, backgrounds) should earn its place. Built-in themes such as theme_minimal() and theme_classic() are a good start. theme() controls individual elements; element_blank() removes one.

RPython



region_le <- gapminder |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(life_expectancy = mean(life_expectancy))

ggplot(region_le, aes(x = life_expectancy, y = fct_reorder(region, life_expectancy))) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey70") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Mean life expectancy (years)", y = NULL)











region_le = gapminder.groupby("region", as_index=False)["life_expectancy"].mean()
order = region_le.sort_values("life_expectancy")["region"]
region_le["region"] = pd.Categorical(region_le["region"], categories=order)

p = (ggplot(region_le, aes(x="region", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_col(fill="#B3B3B3")
     + coord_flip()
     + theme_minimal(base_size=13)
     + theme(panel_grid_major_y=element_blank(),
             panel_grid_minor=element_blank(),
             figure_size=(7, 3.6))
     + labs(x="", y="Mean life expectancy (years)"))
p.show()











With coord_flip() in Python, the grid lines we removed are the ones that run along the bars. Try changing panel_grid_major_y to panel_grid_major_x to see the difference.

title: 7  Labels, titles and annotation
section: 7.6 Worked example: the full makeover Core
text:
7.6 Worked example: the full makeover Core
Here are all the techniques from this part of the course in one figure: sort, grey, highlight, label directly, and write a headline.

RPython



region_le |>
  mutate(focus = region == "Sub-Saharan Africa") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = life_expectancy, y = fct_reorder(region, life_expectancy), fill = focus)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", life_expectancy)),
            hjust = 1.2, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey65", "#D6083B"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(title = "Sub-Saharan Africa trails every other region by over 10 years",
       subtitle = "Mean life expectancy at birth across countries, 2010",
       caption = "Source: Gapminder", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title.position = "plot")











region_le["focus"] = region_le["region"] == "Sub-Saharan Africa"
region_le["label"] = region_le["life_expectancy"].map("{:.1f}".format)

p = (ggplot(region_le, aes(x="region", y="life_expectancy", fill="focus"))
     + geom_col(width=0.7)
     + geom_text(aes(label="label"), ha="right", nudge_y=-1,
                 color="white", fontweight="bold")
     + coord_flip()
     + scale_fill_manual(values=["#A6A6A6", "#D6083B"], guide=None)
     + scale_y_continuous(expand=(0, 0))
     + labs(title="Sub-Saharan Africa trails every other region by over 10 years",
            subtitle="Mean life expectancy at birth across countries, 2010",
            caption="Source: Gapminder", x="", y="")
     + theme_minimal(base_size=13)
     + theme(panel_grid=element_blank(), axis_text_x=element_blank(),
             plot_title=element_text(size=13, weight="bold"),
             figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()











Because the values are written on the bars, the x axis is no longer needed, so we removed its text.

title: 7  Labels, titles and annotation
text:
7.7 Your own theme Extension
If you make many figures, for a thesis or a paper, define your theme once and reuse it. Every figure will then look consistent.

RPython



theme_mine <- function(base_size = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
          plot.title.position = "plot",
          legend.position = "top")
}

# then add + theme_mine() to any plot, or set it for the whole session:
theme_set(theme_mine())




def theme_mine(base_size=13):
    return (theme_minimal(base_size=base_size)
            + theme(panel_grid_minor=element_blank(),
                    plot_title=element_text(weight="bold"),
                    legend_position="top"))

# then add + theme_mine() to any plot, or set it for the whole session:
theme_set(theme_mine())

title: 7  Labels, titles and annotation
text:
7.8 Exercises






ExerciseWrite the labels







Level: 
Take any plot from an earlier chapter and give it a headline title, a subtitle, a caption with the source, and axis labels in plain words with units.






AnswerAnswer







There is no single right answer. Check your title by asking: does it tell the reader what to notice, or only what is plotted? “Income and life expectancy” is a label. “Richer countries live longer, but the gains shrink at the top” is a headline.
















ExerciseLabel the lines







Level: 
Plot life expectancy over time for Brazil, India, Rwanda and the United Kingdom, with direct labels at the end of each line and no legend.






AnswerAnswer








RPython



four <- gap_years |> filter(country %in% c("Brazil", "India", "Rwanda", "United Kingdom"))
ends <- four |> filter(year == max(year))

ggplot(four, aes(x = year, y = life_expectancy, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = country), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.25))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Life expectancy (years)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")











four = gap_years[gap_years["country"].isin(["Brazil", "India", "Rwanda", "United Kingdom"])]
ends = four[four["year"] == four["year"].max()]

p = (ggplot(four, aes(x="year", y="life_expectancy", color="country"))
     + geom_line(size=1.1)
     + geom_text(ends, aes(label="country"), ha="left", nudge_x=1, fontweight="bold")
     + scale_x_continuous(limits=(1960, 2025))
     + labs(x="", y="Life expectancy (years)")
     + theme_minimal()
     + theme(legend_position="none", figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()



























ExerciseAnnotate an event Extension







Level: 
Find another country with a sharp change in life expectancy (try Cambodia or Haiti). Plot it, and add an annotation that explains the event.






AnswerAnswer







Cambodia shows a severe fall in the late 1970s, during the Khmer Rouge regime. Haiti shows a sharp fall in 2010, the year of the earthquake. Use annotate("text", ...) for the label and annotate("segment", ...) with an arrow to point at the event, as in the Rwanda example.

title: 7  Labels, titles and annotation
text:
7.9 Summary






TipKey points




The title is a headline; the subtitle says what is measured; the caption gives the source.
Use plain-language axis labels with units.
Direct labels are usually better than legends.
Annotations explain why the data looks the way it does.
Remove non-data elements that do not help, and reuse a theme for consistency.

8.1 Load packages and data
We also load patchwork in R, which puts plots side by side with | and on top of each other with /. In Python, plotnine has the same operators built in. We cover this properly in Multi-panel figures and export.

text:
RPython



library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

gapminder <- read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv")
gap_years <- read_csv("data/gapminder_1960_2010.csv")

import pandas as pd

title: 8  Honest scales and axes
section: 8.2 When must an axis start at zero? Core
text:
8.2 When must an axis start at zero? Core
It depends on the channel the reader uses.

Bars and areas are read by their length. A bar twice as long looks like twice the amount. If the axis does not start at zero, the lengths lie. Bars always start at zero.
Points and lines are read by their position. The axis can focus on the range where the data is, as long as it is clearly labelled.

In the figure above, the left panel makes a 3% difference look like a fivefold one. The middle panel is honest but makes the difference hard to see. The right panel uses dots, so it can zoom in honestly.
ggplot2 and plotnine start bar axes at zero by default. The danger usually comes from zooming in afterwards.

title: 8  Honest scales and axes
text:
8.3 Zooming without losing data Core
There are two ways to change the range of an axis, and they behave very differently.

Scale limits (scale_y_continuous(limits = ...) or ylim()) remove data outside the range before anything is calculated. Box plots, means and trend lines change.
Coordinate limits (coord_cartesian(ylim = ...)) zoom the view, like a camera. All the data is still used.


RPython



base <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) + geom_boxplot()

removed <- base + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(3000, 5000)) + ggtitle("Scale limits: data removed")
zoomed <- base + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(3000, 5000)) + ggtitle("Coordinate limits: zoomed")

removed | zoomed











base = ggplot(penguins, aes(x="species", y="body_mass_g")) + geom_boxplot()

removed = base + scale_y_continuous(limits=(3000, 5000)) + ggtitle("Scale limits: data removed")
zoomed = base + coord_cartesian(ylim=(3000, 5000)) + ggtitle("Coordinate limits: zoomed")

p = removed | zoomed
p.show()





Look at the Gentoo box. On the left, every penguin heavier than 5,000 g was thrown away before the box was drawn, so the median is wrong. On the right, the box is correct and just cut off by the view. Use coord_cartesian() to zoom.

title: 8  Honest scales and axes
text:
8.4 Breaks and labels Core
Tick labels should be readable without thinking: thousands separators, currency symbols and percentages where relevant.

RPython


The scales package has a helper for every common format.

ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = child_mortality / 1000)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000),
                labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Children who die before age 5")










In Python, a short function that turns numbers into text does the same job.

gapminder["child_mortality_prop"] = gapminder["child_mortality"] / 1000

p = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="child_mortality_prop"))
     + geom_point(alpha=0.5)
     + scale_x_log10(breaks=[1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000],
                     labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + scale_y_continuous(labels=lambda breaks: [f"{b:.0%}" for b in breaks])
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Children who die before age 5")
     + theme(figure_size=(7, 3.8)))
p.show()

title: 8  Honest scales and axes
text:
8.5 Avoid dual axes Extension
A plot with two different y axes, one on each side, lets you make any two lines appear to cross, diverge or move together, simply by choosing the scales. The crossing point means nothing. Use two aligned panels instead, sharing the x axis.

RPython



brazil <- gap_years |> filter(country == "Brazil")

p_income <- ggplot(brazil, aes(x = year, y = income_per_person)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#0072CF") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, subtitle = "Income per person")

p_mortality <- ggplot(brazil, aes(x = year, y = child_mortality)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#D6083B") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, subtitle = "Child deaths per 1,000 births")

p_income / p_mortality +
  plot_annotation(title = "Brazil: incomes rose while child mortality fell")











brazil = gap_years[gap_years["country"] == "Brazil"]

p_income = (ggplot(brazil, aes(x="year", y="income_per_person"))
            + geom_line(size=1, color="#0072CF")
            + scale_y_continuous(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
            + labs(x="", y="", title="Income per person"))

p_mortality = (ggplot(brazil, aes(x="year", y="child_mortality"))
               + geom_line(size=1, color="#D6083B")
               + labs(x="", y="", title="Child deaths per 1,000 births"))

p = p_income / p_mortality
p.show()





Each panel has its own honest axis, and the shared time axis makes it easy to compare when things changed.

title: 8  Honest scales and axes
text:
8.6 Aspect ratio Extension
Stretching or squashing a plot changes how steep lines look. A flat, wide plot makes change look small; a tall, narrow one makes it look dramatic. A good starting point is to choose a shape where the most important lines are at roughly 45 degrees. Set the shape deliberately when you save the figure (see Multi-panel figures and export), rather than accepting whatever your screen gives you.

title: 8  Honest scales and axes
text:
8.7 Exercises






ExerciseSpot the trap







Level: 
A colleague shows you a bar chart of mean reaction time in two groups, 412 ms and 431 ms, with the y axis running from 400 to 440 ms. What would you suggest?






AnswerAnswer







The bars exaggerate the difference: the second bar looks more than twice as long as the first, when the difference is under 5%. Either start the axis at zero, or (better) switch to points showing the individual observations and the means, which can be zoomed in honestly.
















ExerciseZoom correctly







Level: 
Make a scatter plot of penguin flipper length against body mass with a straight trend line. Zoom into body masses between 3,000 and 4,500 g, first with scale limits and then with coord_cartesian(). Does the trend line change?






AnswerAnswer








RPython



base <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

(base + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(3000, 4500))) |
  (base + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(3000, 4500)))











base = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="body_mass_g", y="flipper_length_mm"))
        + geom_point(alpha=0.4)
        + geom_smooth(method="lm"))

p = ((base + scale_x_continuous(limits=(3000, 4500)))
     | (base + coord_cartesian(xlim=(3000, 4500))))
p.show()





With scale limits, the line is fitted only to penguins in the range, so it changes. With coord_cartesian(), the line is fitted to all the data and we just see part of it.

title: 8  Honest scales and axes
text:
8.8 Summary






TipKey points




Bars start at zero; points and lines can zoom in, with clear labels.
Use coord_cartesian() to zoom. Scale limits remove data.
Format tick labels for readers: separators, currency, percentages.
Avoid dual y axes; use aligned panels.
Choose the aspect ratio deliberately.

title: 9  Multi-panel figures and export
section: 9.2 Small multiples or combined plots? Core
text:
9.2 Small multiples or combined plots? Core
There are two kinds of multi-panel figure:

Small multiples: the same plot repeated for different subsets of the data, with shared axes. Use facet_wrap() or facet_grid(). You have met these in earlier chapters.
Combined plots: different plots that together tell one story, such as a distribution, a comparison and a relationship. Use patchwork in R, or the composition operators in plotnine.

title: 9  Multi-panel figures and export
text:
9.3 Combining plots Core
Make each plot separately and store it in an object. Then combine them: | puts plots side by side and / stacks them.

RPython



p_hist <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "grey50", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Count")

p_box <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)")

p_scatter <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = species_cols) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)", colour = NULL)

(p_hist | p_box) / p_scatter +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")








plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") adds the panel letters automatically.



p_hist = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="flipper_length_mm"))
          + geom_histogram(binwidth=3, fill="#7F7F7F", color="white")
          + labs(x="Flipper length (mm)", y="Count", tag="A"))

p_box = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="species", y="body_mass_g"))
         + geom_boxplot()
         + labs(x="", y="Body mass (g)", tag="B"))

p_scatter = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", color="species"))
             + geom_point(alpha=0.8)
             + scale_color_manual(values=species_cols)
             + labs(x="Bill length (mm)", y="Bill depth (mm)", color="", tag="C"))

p = (p_hist | p_box) / p_scatter
p.show()


In plotnine, panel letters are added to each plot with labs(tag=...).









ImportantDesign principle: one figure, one story



A multi-panel figure should still have a single message, with each panel contributing to it. If the panels tell unrelated stories, they are probably separate figures.

title: 9  Multi-panel figures and export
section: 9.4 Saving at the final size Core
text:
9.4 Saving at the final size Core
The most common reason for unreadable figures in papers is that they were made at one size and printed at another. Text, points and lines are drawn at a fixed physical size, so shrinking the image shrinks them too.
Decide the final width first, then save at exactly that size:



Where it goes
Typical width




Single journal column
8 to 9 cm


Full page width
17 to 18 cm


Slide (16:9)
about 25 cm wide, 13 cm tall


A0 poster panel
depends on layout; check at 100% zoom




RPython



p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

ggsave("figures/body_mass.pdf", p, width = 8.5, height = 6, units = "cm")
ggsave("figures/body_mass.png", p, width = 8.5, height = 6, units = "cm", dpi = 600)

For a combined patchwork figure, save the combined object in exactly the same way.



p = (ggplot(penguins, aes(x="species", y="body_mass_g"))
     + geom_boxplot()
     + labs(x="", y="Body mass (g)")
     + theme_minimal(base_size=9))

p.save("figures/body_mass.pdf", width=8.5, height=6, units="cm")
p.save("figures/body_mass.png", width=8.5, height=6, units="cm", dpi=600)

Combined plots made with | and / have the same save() method.



At a journal column width, a base font size of 8 to 10 points usually matches the text of the paper. For slides, use 16 or more.

title: 9  Multi-panel figures and export
text:
9.5 Which file format? Core








Format
Type
Use for




PDF or SVG
Vector: shapes and text, sharp at any size
Papers, posters, theses; editing in Illustrator or Inkscape


PNG
Raster: pixels
Slides, web pages, documents; use 300 dpi or more for print


TIFF
Raster
Only when a journal requires it


JPEG
Raster, lossy
Photographs, not plots: it blurs lines and text



When in doubt, save a PDF for print and a PNG for screens.

title: 9  Multi-panel figures and export
text:
9.6 Reproducible figures Core

Script every figure, including panel letters, labels and annotations. Edits made by hand in other software have to be redone every time the data changes.
Define colours and themes once, at the top of your script or in a shared file, so every figure in a paper or thesis is consistent.
Save with explicit sizes, never by copying from the screen.
Keep the script with the data it uses, ideally in a version-controlled project.

title: 9  Multi-panel figures and export
text:
9.7 Exercises






ExerciseA three-panel figure







Level: 
Using the Gapminder 2010 data, make a figure with three panels labelled A to C: a histogram of life expectancy, a sorted bar chart of mean life expectancy by region, and a scatter plot of income against life expectancy. Save it at full page width (17 cm) as a PDF.






AnswerAnswer








RPython



gapminder <- read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv")

a <- ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.5, fill = "grey50", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Life expectancy (years)", y = "Countries")

b <- gapminder |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(le = mean(life_expectancy)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = le, y = fct_reorder(region, le))) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Mean life expectancy", y = NULL)

c <- ggplot(gapminder, aes(x = income_per_person, y = life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Income per person (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy (years)")

fig <- (a | b) / c + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
fig









ggsave("figures/gapminder_overview.pdf", fig, width = 17, height = 13, units = "cm")




gapminder = pd.read_csv("data/gapminder_2010.csv")

a = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_histogram(binwidth=2.5, fill="#7F7F7F", color="white")
     + labs(x="Life expectancy (years)", y="Countries", tag="A"))

region_le = gapminder.groupby("region", as_index=False)["life_expectancy"].mean()
order = region_le.sort_values("life_expectancy")["region"]
region_le["region"] = pd.Categorical(region_le["region"], categories=order)

b = (ggplot(region_le, aes(x="region", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_col(fill="#7F7F7F")
     + coord_flip()
     + labs(x="", y="Mean life expectancy", tag="B"))

c = (ggplot(gapminder, aes(x="income_per_person", y="life_expectancy"))
     + geom_point(alpha=0.5)
     + scale_x_log10(labels=lambda breaks: [f"${b:,.0f}" for b in breaks])
     + labs(x="Income per person (log scale)", y="Life expectancy (years)", tag="C"))

p = (a | b) / c
p.show()



p.save("figures/gapminder_overview.pdf", width=17, height=13, units="cm")




















ExerciseCheck at final size Extension







Level: 
Open the PDF you saved and view it at 100% zoom, or print it. Is every label readable? If not, increase base_size in your theme, rather than making the figure bigger.






AnswerAnswer







Viewing at 100% is the only reliable check. If the text is too small, increase the base font size of the theme (for example theme_minimal(base_size = 10)) and save again at the same width.

title: 9  Multi-panel figures and export
text:
9.8 Summary






TipKey points




Use facets for small multiples, and patchwork or plotnine composition for combined plots.
Add panel letters in code, not by hand.
Decide the final size first, and save at exactly that size.
Use vector formats (PDF, SVG) for print and PNG for screens.
