title: 10  The makeover challenge
text:
10.1 The challenge
Take one figure and make it better. You can use your own figure, a figure from the critique gallery, or one of the briefs below. By the end you should have a before and an after, and be able to explain every change.
Plan for about 45 minutes, or longer if you are working on your own data.

title: 10  The makeover challenge
text:
10.2 Step by step

1. Headline→ 2. Sketch→ 3. Build→ 4. Test→ 5. Refine→ 6. Export


Write the headline. One sentence: what should the reader take away? Write it before any code.
Sketch two versions on paper. Which better supports the headline?
Build the best sketch. A good order of work is: chart type, then sorting, then grey and highlight, then labels, then the theme.
Test with someone else. Show it for five seconds, hide it, and ask what they remember. Then go through the five questions together.
Refine based on what they said.
Export at the final size, and check it at 100% zoom.

title: 10  The makeover challenge
text:
10.3 Worked example
Here is the makeover sequence from the course, one step at a time. The code for the final version is in Labels, titles and annotation.
Headline: Sub-Saharan Africa trails every other region by over 10 years.

BeforeStep 1Step 2After





Default settings: variable names as labels, alphabetical order, colours and a legend that repeat the axis.







Sort by value and flip to horizontal bars, so names have room and the ranking is visible.







Remove the legend, make everything grey, and highlight the bar the message is about.







Write the headline as the title, add a subtitle and source, label the values directly and remove the axis they replace.

title: 10  The makeover challenge
text:
10.4 Briefs
If you do not have your own figure, choose one of these.






ExerciseBrief 1: income and health







Level: 
Data: gapminder_2010.csv
Audience: a general audience reading a news article.
Task: show that the relationship between income and life expectancy flattens out among richer countries. Highlight one region of your choice.











ExerciseBrief 2: three species







Level: 
Data: penguins.csv
Audience: a conference talk to ecologists. The slide will be on screen for about 30 seconds.
Task: show how body mass differs between species and between sexes. Show the data, not just the means.











ExerciseBrief 3: fifty years of change







Level: 
Data: gapminder_1960_2010.csv
Audience: readers of a journal article.
Task: show how child mortality changed between 1960 and 2010 in each region, and draw attention to one country whose story is different from its region’s. Use small multiples, direct labels and at least one annotation. Export as a PDF at full page width.

title: 10  The makeover challenge
text:
10.5 Giving and receiving feedback
When you test your figure with someone:

Reviewer: start by saying what you took away, before any suggestions. Be specific: “my eye went to the legend first” is more useful than “it’s a bit busy”. Offer options rather than instructions.
Owner: listen and take notes. Resist the urge to explain. If the figure needs explaining, it needs changing.

title: 10  The makeover challenge
text:
10.6 Reflect
When you have finished, write two or three sentences for yourself:

What was the single change that helped most?
What will you do differently next time you make a figure?

title: 10  The makeover challenge
text:
10.7 Summary






TipKey points




Start with the headline, then sketch, build, test and refine.
Work in a sensible order: chart type, sorting, colour, labels, theme.
Test with a fresh pair of eyes and the five questions.
Export at the final size and check at 100% zoom.

title: Figure checklist
text:
Five questions
Use this page to check your own figures and to give feedback to others. Work from the top: there is no point adjusting colours if the message is unclear.

title: Figure checklist
text:
Message. What should someone take away in five seconds?
Audience. Who is it for, and what do they already know?
Chart. Does the chart type fit the question?
Attention. Where does the eye go first? Is that where the message is?
Integrity. Is it honest, readable at its final size, and accessible?








ImportantThe five-second test



Show the figure to someone for five seconds, then hide it. Ask what they remember. If it is not your headline, the figure needs work.

title: Figure checklist
text:
Detailed checklist

Message

I can write the message as one sentence.
The title (or the first sentence of the legend) states that message.
Everything on the figure supports the message; anything that does not has been removed or moved to a supplement.



Audience

The level of detail suits the audience: full detail for a paper, one point for a talk, plain language for the public.
Jargon and abbreviations are explained or removed.
A figure from a paper has been remade for a talk, not copied.



Chart

The chart type matches the question: distribution, comparison, relationship, change or part to whole.
The most important comparison uses position or length, not angle, area or colour.
Continuous data is shown as points or distributions, not only as bars of means.



Attention

Categories are sorted by value, or by their natural order.
Colour is used for a reason; supporting data is grey.
Labels are placed directly on the data where possible, instead of in a legend.
Grid lines, borders and backgrounds are light or removed.



Integrity

Bars start at zero. Zoomed axes use points or lines and are clearly labelled.
Log scales are labelled as log scales.
There are no dual y axes.
The palette suits the data: sequential, diverging or qualitative, and not a rainbow.
The colours work for colour vision deficiency, and colour is never the only cue.
Text is readable at the final size (check at 100% zoom).
Axis labels use plain words and units.
The source of the data is given.
The figure has alt text when it is published online. A good pattern is: chart type, what is plotted, then the message.
The figure is made by a script and can be remade if the data changes.

title: Recipes
text:
Sort bars by value
Short, copyable code for the changes you will make most often. Each recipe assumes you already have a plot stored as p, or a data frame df with a categorical column group and a numeric column value. Replace the names with your own.
In Python, these recipes assume import pandas as pd and from plotnine import *.
Turn alphabetical order into a ranking.

title: Recipes
text:

  geom_col()

title: Recipes
text:
Grey everything, highlight one group
Create a true or false column for the group your message is about.

RPython


df |>
  mutate(focus = group == "Mine") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = fct_reorder(group, value), fill = focus)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey75", "#D6083B"), guide = "none")


df["focus"] = df["group"] == "Mine"

(ggplot(df, aes(x="group", y="value", fill="focus"))
 + geom_col()
 + coord_flip()

section: Label line ends instead of a legend
text:
Label line ends instead of a legend
Make a table of the last point of each line, and draw the labels there.

RPython


ends <- df |> filter(year == max(year))

ggplot(df, aes(x = year, y = value, colour = group)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = group), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.25))) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


ends = df[df["year"] == df["year"].max()]

(ggplot(df, aes(x="year", y="value", color="group"))
 + geom_line()
 + geom_text(ends, aes(label="group"), ha="left", nudge_x=1)
 + theme(legend_position="none"))

Small multiples with context
Draw all the data in grey behind every panel, then each group on top.

RPython


ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(data = select(df, -group), colour = "grey85") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072CF") +
  facet_wrap(~ group)

(ggplot(df, aes(x="x", y="y"))
 + geom_point(data=background, color="#D9D9D9")
 + geom_point(color="#0072CF")

title: Critique gallery
text:
AnswerAnswer








Two unrelated y axes: the point where the lines cross means nothing, because it depends on how each scale was chosen.
Raw variable names as axis labels, and no title or message.
Better: two aligned panels sharing the time axis. See Honest scales and axes.

section: Figure B: Countries by religion and income group
text:
Figure B: Countries by religion and income group

Data: gapminder_2010.csv






AnswerAnswer








A pie with twelve slices, many of similar size, which we cannot compare by angle.
The legend combines two variables, so the colours cannot be decoded.
Better: a stacked or grouped bar chart, or small multiples by religion. See Ranking and ordering.

text:
Figure C: Correlations between Gapminder variables

Data: gapminder_2010.csv






AnswerAnswer








A rainbow palette for a correlation, which needs a diverging palette centred on zero.
Variables in no meaningful order, with rotated raw labels.
Better: a diverging palette with limits of -1 and 1, values written in the tiles, and readable labels. See Colour with purpose.

section: Figure E: Beak depth in four groups of finches
text:
Figure E: Beak depth in four groups of finches

Data: finches.csv






AnswerAnswer








Bars of means with standard errors hide the data.
The y axis is truncated, so the bars exaggerate small differences.
The colour repeats the x axis, and one group appears to be missing because its bar falls outside the truncated axis.
Better: show every point with the mean. See Distributions.

AnswerAnswer








Four channels at once: position, size, colour and shape, plus every country labelled.
Heavy overplotting in the bottom left, because income is on a linear scale.
